# New Snack Line for a Target International Market: A Worked Concept for Japan

Most snack launches in a new market fail the same way: the company exports a product and localizes the label. The flavors are "inspired by" the market, the portions are the home-market portions, and the launch goes through the home-market channel logic. The governing rule for this plan:

> **Don't localize a product. Localize the occasion.** Flavor earns trial; occasion fit earns repeat purchase. Build backward from *when, where, and with what* people snack — then flavor it authentically.

Since the brief doesn't name the market, I'll build the full line for **Japan** — arguably the world's most demanding snack market, and the clearest demonstration of "distinct local tastes." Section 7 shows how the framework transfers to any market.

---

## 1. Read the Market Before Designing Anything

- **Snacking occasions are institutionalized.** *Oyatsu* — the 3pm snack break — is a literal cultural tradition. *Otsumami* are snacks engineered to pair with beer and highballs. *Omiyage* is the obligatory regional gift box you bring colleagues after travel. Three occasions, three different products, three different channels.
- **Seasonality is retail law.** Sakura (Feb–Apr), salt-citrus "heat countermeasure" products (summer), sweet potato/chestnut (autumn), strawberry-chocolate (winter). *Gentei* (limited editions) drive store traffic.
- **Texture is a flavor dimension.** Japanese consumers describe snacks with texture vocabulary — *saku-saku* (light crisp), *fuwa-fuwa* (pillowy soft). Dense, heavy, fatty mouthfeel reads as foreign.
- **Sensory norms differ measurably.** Sweetness runs ~25–30% below US equivalents; salt arrives via umami carriers (soy, miso, dashi) rather than straight sodium; sour and bitter notes (yuzu, ume, matcha) are assets, not risks.
- **The convenience store (*konbini*) is the national trial engine.** ~55,000 stores (7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Lawson) with weekly shelf resets — brutal turnover, but the fastest, cheapest trial loop in global retail.
- **Proof the model works:** Kit Kat Japan (300+ local flavors, gift formats) and Calbee's Jaga Pokkuru (a Hokkaido-only potato snack that became a sold-out must-buy souvenir). Global platform + hyper-local flavor pipeline + giftable format = the winning pattern.

---

## 2. Line Architecture: Three Sub-Lines Built on Three Occasions

One platform brand (working name **"Saku Saku"** — the onomatopoeia for light crispiness; placeholder pending linguistic/trademark screening), three occasion-built sub-lines:

| Sub-line | Occasion | Format logic | Primary channel |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oyatsu** (sweet) | 3pm desk/afternoon break | Individually wrapped minis; clean to eat at a keyboard | Konbini, office vending |
| **Tsumami** (savory) | Evening beer/highball pairing | Bold umami; shareable but portionable | Konbini (beer aisle adjacency), drugstores |
| **Gentei** (limited/gift) | Seasonal moments, travel, omiyage | Rotating regional flavors; boxed sets | Station kiosks, airports, e-commerce |

---

## 3. The Product Concepts

| # | Product | Flavor & hero ingredients | Format | Occasion | Pack / price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Uji Matcha Wafer Minis | Kyoto Uji matcha cream, white-chocolate drizzle | 8 individually wrapped wafers | 3pm desk break | ¥198 |
| 2 | Kinako & Black Sesame Rice Crisps | Roasted soybean flour, kuromitsu (black sugar) drizzle | Baked brown-rice crisps, not fried | Health-leaning afternoon | ¥168 |
| 3 | Yuzu-Honey Madeleine Bites | Kōchi yuzu, domestic honey | 6 soft mini cakes, giftable | Tea time, small gift | ¥248 |
| 4 | Nori-Shio Light Chips | Hokkaido potatoes, aonori seaweed, sea salt | Thin-cut chips | Baseline beer snack | ¥148 |
| 5 | Ume-Shiso Bean Crisps | Pickled plum + shiso on lentil/pea base | Sour-savory crisps | Highball pairing | ¥168 |
| 6 | Miso-Butter Corn Puffs | Hokkaido miso + butter (ramen-shop nostalgia) | Airy puffs | Evening comfort snack | ¥148 |
| 7 | Yuzu-Kosho Pea Snaps | Yuzu chili paste, 8g protein per pack | Baked pea snaps | Functional savory (health shelf) | ¥178 |
| 8 | Kaki-no-Tane Mix | Classic rice cracker + peanut, co-packed with a Niigata senbei maker | Share pouch | Otsumami staple — credibility SKU | ¥198 |
| 9 | Sakura-Adzuki Crisps *(Feb–Apr)* | Sakura white-choc filling, red bean | Limited run | Hanami season | ¥198 |
| 10 | Salt-Lemon Shikuwasa *(Jun–Aug)* | Okinawan shikuwasa citrus + salt | "Heat countermeasure" positioning | Summer hydration-adjacent | ¥168 |
| 11 | Satsumaimo & Kokuto *(Sep–Nov)* | Roasted sweet potato, Okinawan black sugar | Baked bites | Autumn tradition | ¥178 |
| 12 | Regional Omiyage Boxes | Hokkaido butter-corn / Kyoto matcha / Okinawa pineapple-kokuto | 12–16 pc gift boxes, local landmark art | Travel gifting | ¥1,080–1,620 |

SKU #8 deserves emphasis: co-packing the *kaki-no-tane* with a Niigata senbei manufacturer buys instant authenticity — the foreign brand arrives as a guest who did the homework, not a colonizer.
